questions.prompt: For a real symmetric matrix \(A\), the Rayleigh quotient \(R(x) = x^T A x / x^T x\) satisfies
questions.explanation: In the eigenbasis the quotient is a weighted average of the eigenvalues, so it lies between the smallest and the largest. It equals an extreme eigenvalue at the matching eigenvector, not beyond it. Scaling \(x\) cancels in the fraction.

questions.explanation: \(x^T A x = 4+1 = 5\) and \(x^T x = 2\), so \(R = 5/2 = 2.5\). The larger eigenvalue 4 is the maximum, not the value at \((1,1)\). Forgetting to divide by \(x^T x\) leaves 5.

questions.prompt: On a symmetric matrix, the upper bound \(\lambda_{\max}\) of the Rayleigh quotient is attained
options: at a vector orthogonal to every eigenvector
questions.explanation: The weighted average of the eigenvalues equals the largest one only when all the weight sits on that eigenvalue, which is the corresponding eigenspace. The zero vector is excluded because the quotient divides by \(x^T x\). A generic unit vector lands strictly between the extremes when the eigenvalues differ.

questions.prompt: What is the trace of \(\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\)? The trace equals the sum of the eigenvalues.
questions.explanation: The trace is \(5+3 = 8\). The off-diagonal entries cancel out of the trace. The determinant is \(15-1 = 14\), the product of the eigenvalues rather than their sum.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a symmetric matrix with trace equal to the sum of its diagonal</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">5   1</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1   3</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A symmetric 2 by 2 matrix with diagonal entries 5 and 3.

questions.prompt: For a symmetric matrix, the determinant equals
options: the Rayleigh quotient of the all-ones vector
questions.explanation: The characteristic polynomial's constant term makes the determinant the product of the eigenvalues, while the trace is their sum. The Rayleigh quotient of one vector is a single weighted average, not the product.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>symmetric 2 by 2 matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">4   2</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2   4</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with equal diagonal entries and equal off-diagonal entries.

questions.explanation: \(\det = 4-1 = 3\), the product of the eigenvalues 3 and 1. The trace is 4, the sum of those eigenvalues. The off-diagonal entry 1 is not the determinant.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a symmetric matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2   1</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1   2</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A symmetric 2 by 2 matrix with 2s on the diagonal.

questions.prompt: Replacing \(x\) by \(3x\) in the Rayleigh quotient
questions.explanation: Both \(x^T A x\) and \(x^T x\) scale by \(9\), so the ratio is invariant. Multiplying by 3 or by 9 would be right for the numerator or the denominator alone, not for the quotient.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>two arrows from one origin</title><line x1="46" y1="161.7" x2="250" y2="161.7"/><polygon points="250,161.7 243.6,164.4 243.6,159" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="60.1" y1="176" x2="60.1" y2="28"/><polygon points="60.1,28 62.8,34.4 57.3,34.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="248" y="175.7" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="66.1" y="30" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="60.1" y1="161.7" x2="235.9" y2="131.8"/><polygon points="235.9,131.8 230,135.6 229.1,130.2" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="243.9" y="123.8" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x</text><line x1="60.1" y1="161.7" x2="95.2" y2="42.3"/><polygon points="95.2,42.3 96,49.3 90.8,47.7" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="103.2" y="34.3" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">y</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: Two arrows leave the origin with a gap between them.

questions.explanation: \(A(1,0) = (2,1)\), so \(x^T A x = 2\) and \(x^T x = 1\). The quotient is 2. The eigenvalues are 3 and 1, and this vector is neither eigenvector. The determinant 3 is the product of the eigenvalues.

questions.explanation: The eigenvalues are the diagonal entries 4 and 1, so the gap is 3. Their ratio is 4, and their sum is 5. The gap is the width of the interval that contains every Rayleigh quotient.

questions.prompt: For a symmetric positive definite matrix the condition number in the 2-norm is \(\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\). What is that ratio for eigenvalues 4 and 1?
questions.explanation: \(4/1 = 4\). The difference \(3\) is the gap, not the ratio used in the convergence bound for steepest descent. The trace 5 is the sum.

questions.prompt: Power iteration on a symmetric matrix can be read as a method that
options: drives the Rayleigh quotient up toward \(\lambda_{\max}\)
computes the determinant in one matrix-vector product
returns a vector orthogonal to the leading eigenvector
applies only to matrices with a zero eigenvalue
questions.explanation: Each multiplication by \(A\) emphasizes the largest-eigenvalue component, and the Rayleigh quotient of the resulting vector climbs toward \(\lambda_{\max}\). One product does not yield the determinant. The iteration looks for the leading direction, not a vector orthogonal to it.

questions.prompt: On a strongly convex quadratic, a large spread of eigenvalues makes steepest descent slow. A method that avoids that zigzag by taking conjugate directions is
options: a single gradient step of fixed length
replacement of the matrix by its determinant
questions.explanation: Conjugate gradient builds directions that are conjugate in the Hessian inner product and finishes a quadratic in finitely many steps. One gradient step does not cancel the zigzag. The trace and the determinant summarize the eigenvalues but do not generate the directions.
